transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-25 15:00 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Ellis, Priya Anand, Miguel Torres (Redwood); Ava Robinson, Tom Nguyen, Leah Park, Samir Dutta (HelixRetail)

Summary/auto notes: quick post-incident sync to lock down recovery steps and a verification playbook. Some sections auto-generated by Fireflies may be imperfect.

00:00 Jordan Ellis: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll give it a hard 45 minutes, there's a bit to walk through. I pulled together a compressed playbook after the weekend's crashloops.
00:14 Ava Robinson: Yeah thanks Jordan. Quick callout, we had a ~20 minute user-impact window, a lot of 503s, then things recovered after a rolling restart. We captured container core dumps and traces.
00:28 Jordan Ellis: Right. Priya, do you want to run the root cause summary that you and the infra team looked at?
00:35 Priya Anand: Sure. So initial hypothesis — there are two compounding factors. One was memory pressure during long beam/batch requests plus cold KV-cache misses causing a synchronous blocking fill. That bumped tail latency, pod restart churn increased because OOMkiller signals and kubelet restarts.
00:54 Tom Nguyen: When you say "beam/batch" you mean the nightly high-token synthetic traffic? It was during the 02:00 run, correct?
01:03 Priya Anand: Right, the nightly scoring job. Also a small percent of requests had very high context windows and triggered larger kv cache entries (I think some of the prompt templates have exploded tokens).
01:15 Samir Dutta: We also saw a pattern where liveness probe failures happened only after the memory started swapping on the node. The kernel's OOM behaviour made things worse.
01:28 Jordan Ellis: Important: Redwood's runtime should keep a TTL on the cache and async fill to prevent blocking — we had a guard that was mis-configured in that deployment. Priya will walk the config.
01:39 Priya Anand: In this customer's Dedicated pool we found that the async-fill flag was disabled because of an older rollout policy they pinned. So it fell back to synchronous KV population which meant the main inference loop waited on remote cache store. That increased memory footprints temporarily.
01:56 Leah Park: Is that an explicit knob in the config or something the platform auto-applies?
02:03 Priya Anand: It's a per-deployment runtime flag. Newer images default to async fill plus backpressure, older ones needed the flag set. The pinned version in Helix's Dedicated cluster predated that change.
02:15 Ava Robinson: Ok that matches our timeline. What were the restart policies? We felt kube's restart semantics exacerbated the flapping.
02:24 Jordan Ellis: You had a restartPolicy of Always but the readiness and liveness probes were very aggressive — readiness probe failing was causing immediate traffic loss, but kubelet restarts were too frequent which didn't leave time for cache warm up. We suggested bumping initialDelaySeconds and failureThreshold.
02:41 Tom Nguyen: Can you share the suggested numbers? We need a reproducible cookbook.
02:46 Jordan Ellis: Yes. In the playbook: set liveness initialDelaySeconds to 60, timeoutSeconds 5, failureThreshold 5 for this workload; readiness initialDelay 20, failureThreshold 3. Also make sure postStart hooks don't block on remote calls.
03:05 Priya Anand: And enable async-kv-fill, set cache eviction policy to LRU with a capped entry size and soft TTL 30 minutes for large embeddings. Also enable fallback routing: if kv fill latency > 500ms persist on an alternate model variant with smaller memory footprint so you avoid big spikes.
03:25 Ava Robinson: Fallback routing — is that Redwood's built-in policy? How transparent is state transfer?
03:30 Priya Anand: It's a routing policy you can configure. Session stickiness matters — it's per-request, so long running sessions may need explicit eviction. For inference you can fail over to a compatible quantized variant that accepts the same inputs but has lower memory.
03:45 Samir Dutta: During the incident we saw one node enter crashloop while the rest had elevated latency; the autoscaler added pods but they also had cold caches so initial token cost was high. Could we pre-warm or snapshot cache?
03:58 Jordan Ellis: There are two approaches: proactive pre-warm scripts that populate common prefixes in staging at rollout time, or persistent cache volumes for KV store (but that has complexity around invalidation). For now, we recommend pre-warm + smaller bucket expiry to reduce statefulness.
04:18 Tom Nguyen: Ok. Let's talk mitigation for production now — immediate steps we can take that don't require an image update.
04:26 Jordan Ellis: Immediate mitigations: 1) increase readiness/liveness thresholds as discussed; 2) apply traffic-shaping to the nightly batch jobs (rate-limit tokens/parallelism); 3) temporarily lower the batch size in the job to reduce memory spikes; 4) add a canary target to route a small percent to a lower-memory model variant.
04:49 Leah Park: We can do 1 and 2 today. 3 needs coordination with the batch owners but should be quick. 4 needs config change in the routing rule; Miguel, can Redwood push a temporary canary?
04:59 Miguel Torres: Yes we can push a routing adjustment from the control plane; I'll own that if you give access. We'll need an RBAC invite so we can create a canary route in Helix's dedicated control plane.
05:10 Ava Robinson: We'll add Miguel's service account for the control plane operations; security has to sign off but should be fine.
05:16 Jordan Ellis: Great. Another item — you shared core dumps and traces, Priya, what in the artifacts looked most telling?
05:24 Priya Anand: The core dumps show the process was in a memory allocation path inside the tokenizer library at the time of death — some allocations were much larger than expected. We also saw a spike of open file descriptors which matched a leak in one of the adapter threads. The trace pointed to long blocking on remote cache fill in the same timeframe.
05:40 Tom Nguyen: So it's not only KV cache, there may be an adapter leak. Is that in the app code or the runtime shim?
05:48 Priya Anand: Looks like adapter-level bug that binds to the runtime's C-bindings. We've filed an upstream bug and a patch is in review; it's not trivial to roll into production w/out a canary.
05:58 Samir Dutta: That suggests we need the playbook to include a fallback model and an explicit rollback criterion by error rate and OOM count.
06:08 Jordan Ellis: Agreed. Playbook section: "If OOM count > 3 in 5m OR 5xx rate > 5% sustained for 10m -> Trigger automatic rollback to previous pinned model and scale down batch jobs."
06:21 Leah Park: I want the exact kubectl commands and a checklist so oncall isn't guessing.
06:27 Jordan Ellis: We'll include a minimal script: kubectl patch deployment ... then step to drain the node if necessary, and how to roll traffic. We'll include runbook steps with copy-paste commands.
06:39 Priya Anand: Also putting a synthetic probe that simulates long-context requests on staging every rollout helps catch the leak before prod.
06:47 Tom Nguyen: That makes sense. On the security side — when Priya uploads logs, what redaction do we need? We can't share PII.
06:54 Priya Anand: We'll run a sanitization script: strip headers with tokens, redact user IDs, and we only need stack traces, alloc histograms, and config files. We'll not include payload prompts.
07:06 Ava Robinson: Good. On the SLA, we considered temporary burst capacity — can Redwood offer emergency burst GPU capacity for a few hours if we need to spin up duplicate nodes?
07:16 Miguel Torres: We do have a burst pool option in Dedicated — it's a premium operation but doable. We can coordinate on-call escalation. We'll include pricing notes in the follow-up.
07:26 Tom Nguyen: Competitors were mentioned in our postmortem — folks asked whether ManagedInferenceCo had better resilience — any thoughts?
07:33 Jordan Ellis: Every vendor has tradeoffs; our emphasis is making failure modes observable and controllable: faster failover, transparent routing, and the ability to sandbox model variants. We'll add a comparison note in the doc.
07:45 Ava Robinson: Ok let's walk the verification plan — how do we validate recovery actually works end-to-end?
07:50 Jordan Ellis: Step one: run staged crash drill in staging with the exact workload: ramp the batch job to create similar memory/cold-cache profile. Step two: apply playbook mitigations (probe threshold changes, canary routing) and observe whether OOMs drop and 5xxs reduce. Step three: run a canary production deploy with 1% traffic and observe metrics for 48 hours before scaling.
08:12 Priya Anand: We'll instrument a specific metric: kv_fill_latency_p50/p95, process_rss, oom_count, readiness_failures. Also traceability via request id across the stack so you can follow a request across model, cache, and node.
08:28 Samir Dutta: About the persistent KV cache suggestion — we talked about snapshotting; what's the operational cost and invalidation surface?
08:35 Priya Anand: The snapshot approach means you keep a warm store but you need a TTL and a versioning scheme. On deployment you restore the snapshot, but invalidation is a must if model tokenization changes. It's heavier ops, so recommended for very latency-sensitive prod only.
08:51 Leah Park: For now we'll avoid persistent state; pre-warm is simpler.
08:55 Jordan Ellis: Sounds good. Let's capture some phrasing for the postmortem blurb for execs — short, clear: cause, impact, mitigations, next steps. Priya to draft language.
09:05 Priya Anand: Draft: "Root cause: synchronous KV cache population + memory leak in adapter causing OOMs during high-token batch runs. Impact: ~20m user-facing degradation; mitigation: readiness/liveness tuning, canary routing, reduced batch parallelism. Next: patch for adapter leak in review, runbook verification and drills scheduled."
09:29 Ava Robinson: Good. We also discussed ownership for any long-term work — Helix will own rolling out probe changes and running drills; Redwood will own the runtime flag fix and the patch backport plan.
09:45 Jordan Ellis: Yep. We'll produce the playbook doc and a short checklist for oncall, plus a script to automate the kube patches.
09:54 Tom Nguyen: Can we also get a small regression test harness — maybe a GH repo with scripts to run the synthetic long-context workload?
10:01 Priya Anand: Yes, we'll share a small repo with a harness and instructions. It's lightweight.
10:08 Miguel Torres: On contracts, if you want extended log retention for debug traces we need to tweak the Dedicated contract terms — I'll follow up with legal and procurement.
10:17 Ava Robinson: Ok noted.
10:20 Jordan Ellis: Any final Qs?
10:24 Tom Nguyen: One more: how do we verify fallback routing won't affect user session coherence for conversational flows?
10:30 Priya Anand: Fallback is stateless per request; for long-running sessions you should evict session-level KV and rehydrate; for chat you may want to pin sessions to a single model variant until resolution. We'll call that out in the doc.
10:45 Leah Park: Great. Can we get an annotated timeline of the incident included in the artifacts? That helped us a lot during the RCA.
10:52 Priya Anand: We'll produce an annotated timeline with metric snapshots and attach the sanitized traces.
10:58 Jordan Ellis: Ok closing summary — action items recap: Redwood to share playbook + scripts + sanitized artifacts; Helix to run 2 drills and report back; schedule follow-up April 8th. Miguel to start conversation on burst capacity pricing and log-retention amendment.
11:17 Ava Robinson: Thanks all.
11:20 Jordan Ellis: Thanks, we'll follow up via the shared folder and calendar invite. Meeting ends.

Notes/transcription quirks: speaker labels occasionally misaligned, some technical names may be transcribed (e.g., "KV cache" vs "K V cache"), punctuation omitted in places.
